briefing.headline: The model predicts the mandate would raise departures over the next 12 months from about 527 to about 956 out of 5,000, roughly 430 extra leavers (+89%); treat the size as a rough estimate and the direction as fairly reliable.
briefing.most_at_risk: Long-commute employees react worst (+118% leaving), followed by caregivers (+112%) and managers (+104%), because the first two bear the most time and logistics cost and managers both lose flexibility and are asked to police their own teams' badge swipes.
risks: Losses concentrate among managers and experienced staff: modelled long-tenured directors and managers with 8 to 12 years say they will comply but quietly take recruiter calls, so departures may come from people who are hard to replace.

Badge tracking is read as distrust ('tracked like a kid', 'insulting', 'patronizing') even by people with short commutes who otherwise accept three days, so it turns a manageable change into a morale and retention problem.

Many modelled employees say they will comply while starting to look, so attrition may build over months as competitors with flexible policies recruit, not show up right away. Lower engagement among people who stay is also likely, though the simulation did not measure it.
design_changes: Let each team choose its own in-office days instead of fixed company-wide days, so people come in when their colleagues are actually there and can plan caregiving and commutes.
Drop individual badge-swipe reviews with managers, or limit them to aggregate office-use reporting, so managers are not put in the position of policing their own people.

Move exception decisions from VPs to direct managers, using published criteria such as long commutes and caregiving duties, and lengthen the 90-day lead time so affected employees can rearrange care and travel.
briefing.confidence: medium, because every group moves sharply in the same direction and the voices consistently explain why, but the numbers come from only 48 modelled voices weighted to headcount, so the +89% should be read as 'a large increase', not a precise forecast.

subgroup_checks.claim: Bigger rise for mid and senior managers
